source.name: The Fleet of Hannibal Sailing to Spain
source.description:
This portion of the Ancient History to the Reign of Caesar discusses the history of Rome, the long-time adversary of the state of Carthage and the sworn enemy of Hannibal's family. At the tender age of twenty-six, Hannibal was elected commander-in-chief of the Carthaginian army and went on to become one of the greatest military leaders of antiquity. Much of Hannibal's subsequent career was devoted to consolidating Carthage's possessions in Spain, an effort that eventually led to a bitter war with Rome.   
 In this image, Hannibal and his army set sail for Spain against the imposing backdrop of Carthage's fortified walls. The crowned Hannibal sits high up in the ship to the right, elevated above his troops and the only figure whose head rises up above the water. In another ship, elephants stand equipped for battle, evidence of the army's origin on the northern coast of Africa.

ownerReview.en: A crowned Hannibal, soldiers and battle elephants sail before a fortified city. Made more than sixteen centuries after the Second Punic War, this Parisian manuscript casts the ancient conflict in the visual language of medieval kingship, ships and fortifications.

source.name: Necklace with a Bearded Head Pendant
source.description:
The necklace consists of twenty-six hollow gold beads, each about 8 mm in diameter, separated by circlets of small hollow beads. Pairs of spherical beads on either side of the pendant are decorated with "dust" granulation. The central gold spacer is formed of a horizontal cylinder with a hemispherical element below, which forms the cap on a male head; both are ornamented with linear and opposed triangle granulation, The glass pendant head of a man has white skin, slanted blue eyes and raised brows, full red lips, and a blue beard divided into four ringlets. It is likely that the necklace has been recomposed in the modern era.  
Phoenician and Punic glass pendants were imported from the Levant and Carthage (in present-day Tunisia), which maintained close political and commercial ties with Etruria. They are widely dispersed throughout Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and the eastern Mediterranean. The typology of this head, however, is best compared to pendants found in 4th and 3rd century contexts, suggesting that the necklace may have been recomposed in the modern period. The gold beads exemplify the Etruscans’ mastery of granulation, filigree, and other metalworking techniques.

ownerReview.en: The glass head connects Punic craftsmanship with Mediterranean exchange between Carthage, the Levant and Etruria. Its probable Carthaginian origin and later date distinguish it from the older Etruscan gold beads. Their current arrangement is probably a modern recomposition.
ownerReview.zh: 玻璃头像把布匿工艺与迦太基、黎凡特和伊特鲁里亚之间的地中海交流联系起来。坠饰可能产自迦太基，年代晚于伊特鲁里亚金珠；现有装配方式可能形成于近代。

title.en: Carthage: a North African maritime power

summary.en: Carthage developed from an earlier settlement into a major Mediterranean trading power. Its location on the Gulf of Tunis connected North Africa with islands, ports and rival states across the sea. Commercial reach depended on political and military relationships as well as ships and goods. The Punic Wars placed Carthage in prolonged conflict with Rome, ending in the city’s destruction in 146 BCE. A Roman city later rose on the site. This layered history makes Carthage a useful place to distinguish a city, a trading network, an imperial state and the successive communities that occupied the same landscape.
summary.zh: 迦太基由早期聚落发展为地中海贸易强权，突尼斯湾的位置连接北非、岛屿和各地港口。商业影响不仅依靠船只与货物，也依靠政治和军事关系。布匿战争使其长期与罗马冲突，最终于前146年遭毁；后来罗马城市又在原址兴起。这里适合区分城市、贸易网络、帝国国家，以及先后生活于同一地景的不同社区。

dateNote.en: c. 600–146 BCE focuses on the trading-power phase; the city’s foundation belongs to the ninth century BCE.
dateNote.zh: 约前600—146年关注贸易强权阶段；建城则在公元前九世纪。

title.en: Punic Wars: fleets, provinces and conquest
title.zh: 布匿战争：舰队、行省与征服

location.label: Messina / ancient Messana; first-war opening context, not the whole theatre

summary.en:
Rome and Carthage fought three major wars between 264 and 146 BCE. The first developed around Sicily, where local disputes and competing alliances drew in larger powers. Maintaining ships, crews and supplies made the struggle a contest of resources as well as battles. Rome’s victory brought the larger part of Sicily under provincial rule.

The second war extended conflict across the western Mediterranean; the third ended with Carthage’s destruction and the enslavement of survivors. These were separate wars with intervals between them, not uninterrupted fighting for more than a century. Their consequences connect Roman political history to North African cities, maritime work and coerced labour. Polybius explains the opening war through alliances and strategic decisions, but his retrospective narrative cannot stand in for all the people affected. The Sicily point is one entry into this wider history, while the related Carthage record supplies an African anchor.
summary.zh:
罗马与迦太基在公元前264年至前146年之间进行了三次大规模战争。第一次战争围绕西西里展开，地方冲突和相互竞争的联盟把更大的势力卷入其中。船只、船员和补给的维持，使战争既是战场上的较量，也是资源的较量。罗马获胜后，西西里大部被纳入行省统治。

第二次战争把冲突扩展到西地中海；第三次以迦太基的毁灭及幸存者被奴役告终。三次战争之间存在间隔，并非连续交战一个多世纪。其后果把罗马政治史与北非城市、海上劳动及强迫劳动联系起来。波利比乌斯从联盟与战略决策解释战争的开端，但其追述不能代表所有受影响者。西西里点位只是进入这段广阔历史的一个入口，关联的迦太基条目提供非洲的观察点。

dateNote.en: Three wars: 264–241, 218–201 and 149–146 BCE. The enclosing interval includes peace; no front line is mapped.
dateNote.zh: 三次战争分别为公元前264—241、218—201及149—146年。总区间包含和平时期，不绘制战线。

en: Separate wars reshaped Mediterranean political control.
Sicily and Carthage offer different geographic viewpoints.
